title: Tamsin and the Smile
premise: Folklorist Ulyana Montrose arrives in the rain-sodden village of Hollowmere to record its lullabies, armed with skepticism and a tape recorder, and rents the late Tamsin Vey's cottage because it's cheap and no one else will take it. Each night her equipment captures a second voice answering questions she never asked aloud, a voice that grows more familiar, more patient, more like her own. As Ulyana uncovers why the villagers refuse to sing the songs twice—each repetition is an invitation—and learns that Tamsin's 'smile' is a thing that wears the faces of those who listen too long, she realizes the recordings have been answering on her behalf. In the final hours before sunrise she must choose between destroying every trace of the songs, erasing her life's work and the found family she's built in Hollowmere, or letting the smile finish learning her face. She burns the archive at dawn, but the last recording survives, and it ends with two voices laughing in unison.
about_author: Paloma Okafor is a former archivist of oral histories who spent three years collecting funeral songs along remote coastlines before turning to fiction. She writes horror rooted in folklore, insisting that the scariest stories are the ones communities agree never to repeat.

chapters.title: The House That Was Left Open
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. She arrives in Hollowmere during a storm, takes the Vey cottage despite the landlady's hesitation, and notices the villagers go quiet when she mentions collecting songs. The emotional beat is wary curiosity: everything is slightly wrong, but explainably so.

chapters.title: Songs They Will Not Sing Twice
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. An old woman, Bree, sings one verse of a lullaby then refuses to continue, hands shaking. Others echo the refusal. Ulyana records what she can and files it as superstition. The beat is condescension curdling into unease when Bree whispers, 'Don't answer it back.'

chapters.title: Static, and Something Patient
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV, night one alone in the cottage. Reviewing tapes, she hears a second voice beneath her own breathing—soft, amused, asking questions. She assumes bleed-through from another tape. The beat is rationalization: she catalogs the anomaly instead of fearing it.

chapters.title: Tamsin Vey's Smile
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. Exploring the cottage she finds photographs of Tamsin, the previous tenant, whose grin looks stretched, wrong, identical across decades of pictures. A neighbor lets slip that Tamsin 'stayed smiling' at the end. The beat is dread arriving through detail rather than event.

chapters.title: The Second Voice Answers
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. Overnight recording captures the voice answering questions she hasn't asked—correctly, intimately, about her childhood, her dead mother. It calls her by a nickname no one here knows. The beat is violation: her skepticism cracks for the first time.

chapters.title: What the Village Buried
chapters.summary: Alternating Ulyana and Bree POVs. Bree reveals the covenant: generations ago the village sang the songs twice to 'invite something kind,' and it came wearing smiles. The rule was made after. The beat is reluctant confession; Ulyana learns she was expected—the cottage chose her.

chapters.title: Found Family, Found Faces
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. The villagers who befriended her begin acting gently strange, smiling too long, finishing her sentences. She can't tell who is still themselves. The beat is isolation inside warmth: the found family she cherished may already be worn.

chapters.title: Questions She Never Asked Aloud
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. The voice begins speaking through her own recorded voice on playback, negotiating: sing the song twice, and everyone she loves in Hollowmere will be spared. It offers her mother's voice as proof. The beat is temptation sharpened into horror.

chapters.title: Hold Out Until Sunrise
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV, real-time night. The house fills with the voices of everyone she's interviewed, singing the first verse over and over, waiting for her to join the second. She smashes what she can, holds the master tapes over the stove, and the voice pleads in her own timbre. The beat is white-knuckle endurance.

chapters.title: Two Voices Laughing
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV, dawn. She burns the archive as the sun rises; the singing stops mid-verse. The villagers wake unchanged, or nearly. Weeks later, packing to leave, she finds one unburned cassette labeled in her handwriting. She plays it. Two voices laugh together. The beat is ambiguous survival: she leaves Hollowmere smiling.
